Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 72
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: South Eastern Asian
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Refugee Aid Worker
  trauma_type: Terrorism
  pcl5: 53

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Maladaptive Strategies: Rumination: Self-Blame: repeatedly blame myself for what happened, Avoid Driving: Driving or being a passenger in a vehicle, Avoid Conflict: Any situation that might involve disagreement or confrontation
  Threat: Safe Zone Only: I only feel safe in a very limited number of places, Startle to Sounds: I jump or startle at ordinary sounds that would not bother most people, Hypervigilance: Being superalert or watchful or on guard
  Memory: Story Feels Unreal: The memory is so extreme it is hard to believe it actually happened to me, Visual Memories: My memories of the frightening event are mostly pictures or images., Auditory Recall: When I have memories of what happened I sometimes hear things in my head that I heard during the frightening event.

Vignette:
Mr. Tran is a 72-year-old South Eastern Asian male who has been working as a refugee aid worker for over three decades. He is married and has a deep commitment to his work, which involves helping refugees find safety and support in their new homes. Mr. Tran experienced a traumatic event involving terrorism when he was caught in the middle of an attack at a refugee camp two years ago. On that fateful day, Mr. Tran was working at one of the camps where refugees were receiving food and medical supplies. Suddenly, there was a loud explosion followed by gunfire. The scene turned chaotic as people screamed and ran for cover. Mr. Tran vividly remembers the visual images of panic-stricken faces, the sound of shattering glass, and the distant echoes of gunshots. He recalls feeling a deep sense of responsibility to protect those around him but ultimately found himself unable to prevent the harm that befell many refugees. Since the attack, Mr. Tran has been grappling with intense self-blame. He repeatedly questions why he could not have done more to prevent the tragedy. This rumination consumes much of his mental energy, and he often isolates himself, feeling like a failure for not being able to save lives. His sense of guilt is so profound that it influences how he approaches his work now. He avoids driving or even riding as a passenger in vehicles because he associates these activities with the risk of encountering another attack. Mr. Tran also tries to avoid situations where there might be conflict, stemming from a fear of not being able to control or de-escalate any potentially dangerous scenarios. This avoidance has led him to decline many opportunities for community outreach and support groups, further isolating him both professionally and personally. The trauma has profoundly altered Mr. Tran’s sense of safety. He now feels secure only in very limited places—his home and a few trusted locations where he believes he is less likely to encounter danger. Any other environment seems fraught with potential threats. Ordinary sounds that would not normally bother most people, such as the sound of doors slamming or distant sirens, cause him to jump and startle frequently. Mr. Tran's hypervigilance has become a constant state of being. He is always on high alert, constantly scanning his environment for signs of danger. This hyper-awareness makes it difficult for him to relax or enjoy moments without anticipating some impending threat. The memories of the attack are vivid and intrusive. The visual images of that day replay in his mind with such intensity that he struggles to believe they actually happened. He hears the sounds of gunfire and screaming as if they were occurring again, which compounds his distress. These auditory and visual flashbacks disrupt his daily life, often causing him to withdraw from social interactions and activities. Over time, Mr. Tran’s avoidance behaviors have taken a toll on both his work and personal relationships. His reluctance to engage with the community has led to reduced support for the refugees he serves, and his wife notices that he is distant and preoccupied, affecting their once-strong bond. Despite these challenges, what finally brought Mr. Tran to seek help was an overwhelming sense of hopelessness. He realized that without intervention, his trauma would continue to erode his ability to function and provide support to those in need. He is most afraid of losing himself completely and becoming a burden rather than a source of strength for others. Mr. Tran hopes that with therapy, he can regain some semblance of peace and find ways to manage his symptoms without compromising his commitment to helping refugees. His journey towards healing is one where he seeks not only relief from his current suffering but also the possibility of rediscovering his sense of purpose and connection to those around him.
